# Lakkhaṇa Sutta (DN 30 (PTS DN iii 142))

**ID:** DN 30 (PTS DN iii 142)
**Section:** Dīghanikāya (dn)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Lakkhaṇa Sutta
**PTS:** DN iii 142
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0103m.mul6.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Lakkhaṇa Sutta* ("The Marks of a Great Man", DN 30) is the thirtieth discourse of the *Dīghanikāya* [Dhammapala et al. 1984]. Drawing upon the ancient Indian concept of the thirty-two physical marks of a "Great Man" (*mahāpurisa*), the sutta begins by outlining the two potential destinies open to an individual possessing them: either becoming a wheel-turning universal monarch (*cakkavattin*) or a fully awakened Buddha [Cantwell 2010; Dhammapala et al. 1984; Anālayo 2017]. The discourse explains in detail how each bodily mark was karmically generated by the virtuous deeds and spiritual qualities perfected by Gautama as a bodhisattva in his previous lives [Cantwell 2010; Anālayo 2017]. For example, the wheel-marks on his feet are linked to his accomplishment of the four assemblies of disciples, while his smooth, dust-resistant skin is traced to his past habit of approaching ascetics and brahmins for instruction [Anālayo 2016]. Structurally, the text alternates between prose sections that examine the marks singly, in pairs, or in triads, and explanatory verse restatements introduced by quotation formulas such as *tatth' etaṃ vuccati* [Winternitz 1933; Dhammapala et al. 1984; Anālayo 2017].

Full parallels are preserved in the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* (MĀ 59, *Discourse on the Thirty-two Marks*, likely of Sarvāstivāda provenance) and the Sanskrit *Arthaviniścayasūtra* (chapter 26), with partial parallels found in DN 33, DĀ 9, T 12, and Sanskrit fragments [Anālayo 2017].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Full parallels: MA 59 三十二相
- Resembling parallels: Arv 26 Dvā-Triṁśan-Mahā-Puruṣa-Lakṣaṇāni; DN 33 (PTS DN iii 207) Saṅgīti Sutta; DA 9 眾集; SHT Sutta 10; T 12 大集法門
- Mentioned in: Mil 5.2.8 Abhejjaparisapañha; Kv 12.3 Saddovipākotikathā; Kv 4.7 Lakkhaṇakathā; Mil 7.6.7 Vagguliṅgapañha; Mil 5.5.5 Buddhaaviheṭhakapañha

**Sources**

- [Anālayo 2017] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Buddhapada and the Bodhisattva Path (2017) — Details on the two destinies, bodhisattva karma leading to physical marks, prose-verse alternation, and the Chinese Madhyama-āgama parallel (MĀ 59).
- [Cantwell 2010] Cathy Cantwell, Buddhism: The Basics (2010) — Context on the ancient Indian signs of a Great Man and their elaboration in DN 30 as reflecting inner virtues.
- [Dhammapala et al. 1984] Gatare Dhammapala, Richard Gombrich, K. R. Norman, eds., Buddhist Studies in Honour of Hammalava Saddhatissa (1984) — Discussion of the 32 marks, the alternative outcomes of Cakkavattin or Buddha, and treatment of marks singly or in groups.
- [Anālayo 2016] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Foundation History of the Nuns’ Order (2016) — Specific karmic explanations in the text: dust not adhering to skin and wheel-marks on soles relating to the four assemblies.
- [Winternitz 1933] Maurice Winternitz, A History of Indian Literature, Vol. II (1933) — Form of stanzas introduced by quotation phrases such as tatth' etaṃ vuccati.
